clue.text: Obscure European crops under discussion

indicators.note: something under discussion is being talked about, so we go by how the words are spoken rather than spelt

blocks.note: E is the standard abbreviation for European
to crop hair or a hedge is to clip it; said after the E, this sounds like the second part of the word

explanation.surface: A European politician's policy on crops is being debated somewhere obscure.
explanation.walkthrough: Say E plus CLIPS out loud and you hear ECLIPSE (ih-KLIPS). 'Obscure' is a verb here, not an adjective.
explanation.definitionFit: To eclipse something is to block it from view or overshadow it, which is what obscuring means as a verb.

clue.text: Poor quality pile I donated to church

definitions.note: the answer is a noun or adjective meaning a cheap, shoddy item

indicators.note: what is donated to an institution goes into it, so one group of letters is placed inside another

blocks.note: a pile is a heap
taken as written
CE is the Church of England

explanation.surface: Someone hands a heap of shoddy goods to their local church as a donation.
explanation.walkthrough: HEAP and I go together inside CE, the usual crossword abbreviation for the Church of England.
explanation.definitionFit: A cheapie is an informal word for something inexpensive and shoddy, so it describes goods of low standard.

clue.text: Home prepared as part of a larger picture

blocks.note: to be in is to be at home
something set is ready or prepared

explanation.surface: A house is made ready for a role within a bigger painting or scene.
explanation.walkthrough: IN for 'home' is a standard crossword equivalence: if you are in, you are at home.
explanation.definitionFit: An inset is a small image or map placed within a bigger one, such as a detail box on a map.

clue.text: They are quick to get more on your plate

blocks.note: first meaning: tiny units of time that pass in a flash
second meaning: a second helping of food

explanation.surface: Some diners are fast to go back for an extra helping at the buffet.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests greedy eaters rushing back; the first part instead means very short units of time.
explanation.definitionFit: Seconds are both brief units of time on a clock and an extra helping of food served after the first.

clue.text: Title of No 1 fashion

blocks.note: 'number one' is a childish British euphemism for urinating, a pee
the rage is the current fashion, as in 'all the rage'

explanation.surface: A heading naming the top trend of the season.
explanation.walkthrough: 'No 1' looks like a chart position, but in British nursery talk 'number one' means a wee, so it gives PEE.
explanation.definitionFit: A peerage is the rank and title of a British noble such as a lord, earl or baron.

clue.text: Refer to setter getting promoted — it makes you sick

indicators.note: in a down clue, being promoted means going up, so the letters read from bottom to top

blocks.note: to cite a source is to refer to it
the setter refers to themselves as me

explanation.surface: Mentioning the puzzle-maker's career advancement is enough to turn anyone's stomach.
explanation.walkthrough: CITE ME, read upwards in this down entry, gives the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: An emetic is a substance or drug that induces vomiting, so it is something that causes nausea.

clue.text: Picks up something essential to actual practice

indicators.note: what is essential to a thing sits at its core, so one word goes in the middle of another

blocks.note: to pick up a sound is to hear it
actual means real

explanation.surface: Someone notices what really matters in day-to-day practice.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Picks up' looks like collecting, but here it means catching a sound; 'something essential to' puts it at the heart of the next word.
explanation.definitionFit: A rehearsal is a practice run of a play, concert or speech before the real performance.

clue.text: Old dance music provided excessive content

indicators.note: content is what is held within, so one word sits inside the other

blocks.note: to provide is to give, past tense gave
OTT stands for over the top, meaning excessive

explanation.surface: Music for an old-fashioned dance was supplied with far too much in it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Content' reads like 'satisfied' but is the noun: what is held inside. OTT, short for over the top, is common British slang.
explanation.definitionFit: The gavotte is an old French court dance, and also the name for music written in its rhythm.

clue.text: Clowns more put out, as it could mean fewer kids

indicators.note: out can mean disordered or not in its proper state, so the letters are thrown into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Clowns get more annoyed because their act might mean fewer children turn up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Put out' looks like a phrase meaning annoyed, but 'out' alone is the signal and 'put' is part of the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A man with reduced fertility is less likely to father children, so it may result in a smaller family.

clue.text: Joins with European dissidents supporting their leaders

indicators.note: the leaders of words are their front letters, so only the initials are kept

blocks.note: W is an abbreviation for with
E is the abbreviation for European
the initial letters of these two words

explanation.surface: Someone sides with European rebels who back the people in charge of them.
explanation.walkthrough: W for 'with' is a common abbreviation, as in a recipe or note.
explanation.definitionFit: To wed is to marry, so a person who weds another unites with them in matrimony.

clue.text: Shuts up unfinished harbour — it could have been very dangerous

definitions.text: it could have been very dangerous
definitions.note: the answer is a noun phrase for a narrow escape

indicators.note: something unfinished is missing its end, so the final letter is dropped

blocks.note: to shut up a shop is to close it
a haven is a harbour

explanation.surface: Someone closes a half-built port that would have been a serious hazard.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is a whole remark, the kind of thing you say after a near miss, standing in for the phrase naming it.
explanation.definitionFit: A close shave is a narrow escape from disaster, the moment when things nearly went badly wrong.

clue.text: Heads spinning when working, to be precise

indicators.note: something spinning turns round, so the letters face the other way

blocks.note: heads are tops, as the top of a page
a machine that is working is on

explanation.surface: Someone's head spins whenever they are at work, if you want the exact truth.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Heads' is not the body part but the upper parts of things; 'to be' simply joins wordplay to definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Spot on is an informal British expression meaning exactly right or accurate.

clue.text: Steer clear of workers — they are quite tight

blocks.note: to skip something is to avoid it
worker ants are the classic crossword workers

explanation.surface: Advice to avoid certain employees because they are rather stingy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tight' suggests mean with money, but it describes close-fitting clothing.
explanation.definitionFit: Ski pants are close-fitting stretch trousers, often with a stirrup under the foot, so they cling to the legs.

clue.text: Jail drug dealer masquerading as clerk

blocks.note: pen is short for penitentiary, a prison
a pusher is someone who sells drugs

explanation.surface: A dealer in prison pretends to be an office worker.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Masquerading as' joins the wordplay to the definition, saying the combination appears as the clerk.
explanation.definitionFit: A pen pusher is a dismissive term for an office worker who does routine paperwork.

clue.text: Become breathless over suggestive gestures — it's farcical!

blocks.note: to pant is to gasp for breath
O is the cricket scoring abbreviation for an over
to mime is to suggest something by gesture alone

explanation.surface: Someone gasps at a lewd gesture and declares the whole thing ridiculous.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Suggestive' hints at innuendo but simply means gestures that suggest meaning. A pantomime is a British Christmas stage show full of slapstick.
explanation.definitionFit: A pantomime is an absurd, chaotic situation as well as a slapstick show, so a farcical affair can be called one.

clue.text: Guide female into old city

indicators.note: putting one thing into another places it within, so these letters go inside

blocks.note: Ur is the ancient Mesopotamian city
she is the female pronoun

explanation.surface: An instruction to lead a woman into a historic town.
explanation.walkthrough: UR, the biblical city of Abraham, is the crossword's favourite ancient city.
explanation.definitionFit: To usher someone is to escort or lead them to their place, as an attendant in a theatre does.

clue.text: Move around and avoid tension

blocks.note: to shun is to avoid
T is the symbol for tension in physics

explanation.surface: Advice to keep moving and steer clear of stress.
explanation.walkthrough: SHUN plus T. 'Move around' reads as wander about, but means push something from place to place.
explanation.definitionFit: To shunt is to push or shift something to another position, as railway wagons are moved between tracks.

clue.text: In discussion, don't reveal charge to provide water

indicators.note: words in a discussion are spoken, so we take their sound rather than spelling

blocks.note: to hide is to not reveal, and a rate is a charge

explanation.surface: During talks, a supplier keeps quiet about the price of water.
explanation.walkthrough: HIDE RATE, said quickly, is indistinguishable from the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: To hydrate something is to supply it with fluid, as a drink restores moisture to the body.

clue.text: Illegally supplying 3G in slum complex

indicators.note: something complex is tangled and intricate, so the letters are jumbled up

blocks.note: three Gs
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone illegally sells mobile phone signal in a run-down housing estate.
explanation.walkthrough: '3G' looks like the mobile network, but it means three letter Gs. 'Complex' reads as a housing block, yet it signals the jumble.
explanation.definitionFit: Smuggling is moving goods across borders or into places unlawfully, which is a form of illicit provision.

clue.text: Nasty old cops stage trouble at post office

indicators.note: trouble stirs things up and disturbs them, so these letters are disordered

blocks.note: taken as written
PO is the abbreviation for post office

explanation.surface: Unpleasant police officers cause a disturbance at the local post office.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stage trouble' reads as police causing a scene; 'stage' is the letters and 'trouble' the signal.
explanation.definitionFit: The Gestapo was the secret state police of Nazi Germany, notorious for brutality, hence a historical and sinister force.

clue.text: UN store destroyed? It's uncertain

indicators.note: something destroyed is wrecked and broken apart, so the letters are rebuilt differently

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Was the United Nations warehouse wrecked? Nobody can say for sure.
explanation.walkthrough: UN looks like the United Nations but is just two letters of the mix.
explanation.definitionFit: Being not sure means lacking confidence or doubting, which is exactly what being uncertain is.

clue.text: Holy day starts Easter vigil abroad

indicators.note: starts are the opening letters of words, so only the initials are kept

blocks.note: D is the abbreviation for day
the opening letters of these two words
to be abroad is to be out and about

explanation.surface: A religious festival begins with an Easter night-watch held overseas.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Holy day' wants to be read together as a feast; 'Holy' alone is the definition and 'day' gives D. Abroad here means outdoors, out and about.
explanation.definitionFit: Devout describes someone deeply religious and pious, close in sense to saintly or godly.

clue.text: Do evil to criminal? Count me in

indicators.note: something criminal is crooked, bent out of the proper order, so these letters are rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone invited to harm a crook eagerly volunteers to join in.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Criminal' looks like a noun for the victim, but it is the adjective signalling the mix.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are eager informal replies accepting an invitation, saying the speaker wants to join the activity.

clue.text: Dirty dog hiding in empty sty

indicators.note: an empty word has lost its insides, leaving only its outside letters
something hiding in a place is concealed within it, so one piece goes inside

blocks.note: the first and last letters
a mutt is a mongrel dog

explanation.surface: A filthy dog hides in a pigsty that has no pigs.
explanation.walkthrough: MUTT goes between the outer letters of STY. 'Dirty' sounds like the dog's state, but means rude.
explanation.definitionFit: Smutty describes indecent or crude talk and jokes, the sense in which a dirty joke is obscene.

clue.text: Ready to participate in elevating section in rear of pub

indicators.note: a section is a piece cut from inside something, so the letters lie within the phrase
elevating means lifting up, and in a down entry that reads bottom to top

blocks.note: the run of letters spanning the three words

explanation.surface: Someone is keen to join the party being raised in the back room of the pub.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters hide across 'reaR OF PUb' and read upwards in this down entry.
explanation.definitionFit: Being up for something is an informal phrase meaning willing and keen to join in an activity.

clue.text: State recycling African oil

indicators.note: recycling breaks material down and remakes it, so the letters are reformed into something new

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A country or government reprocesses oil from Africa.
explanation.walkthrough: 'State' looks like a nation or a verb meaning declare; it is an American state.
explanation.definitionFit: California is one of the fifty United States, on the Pacific coast of America.

clue.text: Fine gold cross is not genuine

blocks.note: F is the pencil-grade abbreviation for fine
Au is the chemical symbol for gold
an X is a cross

explanation.surface: A delicate golden crucifix turns out to be a fake.
explanation.walkthrough: F, AU and X in sequence. Each piece is a standard abbreviation or symbol.
explanation.definitionFit: Faux is borrowed from French for false and describes imitation materials such as fake fur or leather.

clue.text: Relations more relaxed where shelter's surrounded by river

indicators.note: something surrounded by another is enclosed on all sides, so it sits inside

blocks.note: the Dee is a river in Scotland, and another in Wales and England
a tent is a shelter; the 's is 'is'

explanation.surface: A family gets on better when camping beside a riverbank.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Relations' suggests relatives; it means diplomatic relations. The Dee is a British river.
explanation.definitionFit: Détente is the easing of hostility between nations, as in the Cold War thaw between superpowers.

clue.text: One's concerned if Democrat ousts Republican, becoming more verbose

indicators.note: to oust is to push someone out and take their place, so one letter replaces another

blocks.note: D is the abbreviation for Democrat
R is the abbreviation for Republican
wordier means using more words

explanation.surface: A worried observer of American politics notes speeches get longer when the Democrats replace the Republicans.
explanation.walkthrough: The wordplay runs backwards: put D in place of the answer's second R and you get WORDIER. So the answer is WORDIER with R back where D was.
explanation.definitionFit: A worrier is a person who frets, so 'one's concerned' describes them as someone who is anxious.
